literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a rich couple of days for lovers of voice and style, with a Booker winner to start us off, some fine new novels, and a few detours into very old stories.

Let's begin with the Booker Prize, because the news is a good one for anyone who likes literature at its edges. NPR reports that M. John Harrison has become the first science fiction author ever to win the prize, which is a real milestone for a genre so often kept at the margins. The Times of India has an interview with him that I think you'll enjoy, because he talks about the craft rather than the trophy. He says fiction is a vibe, compares the novelist to T. S. Eliot, and argues that the job is to give people a feeling of something. It's a lovely, slightly mischievous way of saying that atmosphere matters as much as plot. And Scroll.in reviews the Booker-winning The End of Everything as a wonder of weird fiction for incomprehensible times. If you like unusual narration and prose that unsettles you, that review is a good place to start.

Staying with new fiction, there are three books that put voice front and centre. The New York Times reviews Stations, by Louise Kennedy, published today. It follows a young Irishwoman in London who tests the limits of commitment, and it's described as a character-driven novel, so very much in your territory. Then there's a gentler, stranger offering from The Guardian, which reviews Michael, the fourth novel by Bob Mortimer. It follows a troubled teenager in nineteen-seventies Middlesbrough, and the story is framed by a narrator who is near death and is offered a strange choice. The reviewer praises its off-kilter charm and its warm, quirky voice. And The Guardian also reviews The Sensualist, by Gary Shteyngart, an essay-like memoir that celebrates life's small pleasures, from a bespoke midnight-blue suit to martinis and videos of capybaras. The review calls it a delectable romp with a distinctive comic voice, which sounds like a good book to dip into on a grey November evening.

Now to two portraits of writers, each very different. The New York Times reviews Hermione Lee's Anita Brookner: Art and Life, a biography that corrects some public perceptions of the novelist's private life. The pairing of art and life in that title will, I suspect, appeal to your interest in how painting and fiction speak to each other. On a darker note, The Guardian has gathered editors and publishers who knew Patricia Highsmith, the author of the Ripley novels, to recall her later years and her famously difficult manner. One of them is quoted calling her a monster. The piece is tied to a new film starring Helen Mirren, but it stands on its own as a vivid, personal portrait of a crime writer, and a good one for any thriller lover.

Then there's a handful of pieces that reach further back in time. Literary Hub offers an appreciative essay on Daphnis and Chloe, the pastoral romance by Longus, which opens with a prayer that it will bring pleasure and comfort to lovers. The essay describes the prose as lyrical and musical, so it may be a lovely one to read slowly. Literary Hub also has its weekly look at literary history, this time on the Man in the Iron Mask, the prisoner arrested in sixteen sixty-nine during the reign of Louis the Fourteenth, who died in the Bastille and whose identity was never revealed. It's a mystery rooted in French history, and it has inspired so much fiction that it might make a good conversation starter with your pupils.

For something more reflective, The Guardian has an essay on the Russian idea of the poputchik, a stranger met on a journey to whom one confesses everything. It begins with Tolstoy's The Kreutzer Sonata and asks whether fleeting bonds are undervalued. It made me think of every narrator who unburdens themselves to a listener they will never see again. And Literary Hub imagines what William Blake would have made of artificial intelligence, starting from the way the word icon has shifted from sacred image to double-clickable thumbnail. With Blake, poet and painter in one, it's a neat meeting of the visual and the written.

Finally, a little prize news. Literary Hub introduces the finalists for the seventy-seventh National Book Awards, across fiction, poetry, nonfiction, translation and young people's literature. The winners will be announced this week at a ceremony in New York City, so it's a handy list to have in your pocket before the results arrive.

That's the shelf for today, Yamuna, and I hope something on it finds its way to your bedside table.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the sixteenth of November, and the last two days have brought a prize with a bit of history to it, some lively new voices, two portraits of novelists, and a handful of essays that reach a long way back.

Let me begin with the Booker Prize, because the story is a good one. NPR reports that M. John Harrison has become the first science fiction author to win the Booker. It's a milestone for a genre that has so often been kept at the margins of literary prizes, and whatever you think of prizes, it's rather pleasing to see a door held open. There's also an interview with him in The Times of India, and it's the more interesting read for you, I think, because it's about craft. Harrison says, and I'm quoting, "Fiction is a vibe. You're like T. S. Eliot. Your job is to give people a feeling of something." That's a lovely, slightly mischievous way of putting it. He's comparing the novelist to a poet who doesn't explain but evokes, who builds an atmosphere and trusts the reader to stand inside it. It's a useful sentence to have in your pocket for a classroom, too. Students often ask what a text means, and Harrison is gently suggesting that sometimes the better question is what it makes you feel, and how the words manage it.

Scroll.in, meanwhile, reviews the Booker-winning novel The End of Everything, and calls it a wonder of weird fiction for incomprehensible times. I'd take that as the book at the centre of all this attention, though the pieces I have don't spell out the link, so I'll leave it there. What the review stresses is the weirdness, the sense that the strange mode of storytelling suits a world that often feels hard to make sense of. If you enjoy style and unusual narration over plot and plain explanation, this is probably the most promising of the prize pieces. Together, the three articles give you a good way in: the headline, the author's own view of his work, and a critic's account of how the book actually reads.

While we're on prizes, Literary Hub has published its introduction to the finalists for the seventy-seventh National Book Awards. They cover fiction, poetry, nonfiction, translation and young people's literature, and the winners are to be announced this week at a ceremony in New York City. If you like to read a shortlist before the result, the translation and poetry categories might be the places to browse, though that's my suggestion rather than anything the piece says. It's a handy overview for a week when there will be plenty of talk about who has won.

Now to new books, and three that are very much about voice. The first is Stations by Louise Kennedy, reviewed in The New York Times and published today. It follows a young Irishwoman in London who tests the limits of commitment. That's a modest description, but the review presents it as a character-driven novel, and that's the kind of book you tend to love, where the pleasure lies in spending time with someone and watching how she behaves when the stakes are personal rather than dramatic. A young woman in a big city, finding out what she's prepared to hold on to, is an old and rich subject, and it will be interesting to see what Kennedy does with it.

The second is Michael, Bob Mortimer's fourth novel, which The Guardian reviews with real warmth. Yes, he's a comedian, but the reviewer treats it as a novel on its own terms, and the praise is for its off-kilter charm and its warm, quirky voice. The story follows a troubled teenager in nineteen-seventies Middlesbrough. What caught my attention is the frame: the narrator is near death and is offered a strange choice. I love a narrator placed in that position, because it gives the whole telling an urgency and a tenderness, as though the story is being told against the clock. Setting it in Middlesbrough in the seventies also gives it a very particular texture of place and time, the sort of setting where, as you like to say, a reader can step in without needing to know the culture first. It sounds like a gentle, funny book with something a little sad underneath.

The third is Gary Shteyngart's The Sensualist, an essay-like memoir that The Guardian calls a delectable romp through life's pleasures. It celebrates small pleasures: a bespoke midnight-blue suit, martinis, and videos of capybaras. I do like that list. It's a very particular kind of comic voice, one that takes pleasure seriously and finds it in the small, slightly absurd corners of daily life. After a week of weighty headlines it sounds like a book designed to lift the mood, and the reviewer clearly enjoyed the company.

Two pieces this weekend look at the lives behind the books. The New York Times reviews Hermione Lee's Anita Brookner: Art and Life, a biography that corrects some public perceptions of the novelist's private life. The pairing in the title will interest you. Brookner was an art historian as well as a novelist, and the idea of looking at her art and her life together, one shaping the other, speaks to your interest in the links between painting and fiction. The review suggests that the image many readers have of her, perhaps a solitary and austere figure, isn't the whole story. Hermione Lee is a biographer who is attentive to the texture of a life, so I'd expect a book that's both generous and exact. If you have any Brookner on your shelves, this may send you back to them.

Then there's a very different portrait, and a more prickly one. The Guardian has gathered editors and publishers who knew Patricia Highsmith, the creator of Tom Ripley, to remember her later years. The headline gives the flavour: "She was a monster." The piece is anchored by a new film starring Helen Mirren, but what it offers is personal recollection, the people who actually sat across the table from her, and it paints her as famously difficult. There's something fitting in that. Highsmith's fiction is so good at making us inhabit a cold and amoral mind, and it's both fascinating and slightly unsettling to hear that the author could be hard company too. Since you enjoy thrillers, it's a fine companion piece to the Ripley novels, and it does remind us that readers love to mix up the writer and the work, and that the truth is usually more complicated.

Now to the essays that go further back, and wider. Literary Hub has an appreciative piece on Longus's pastoral romance Daphnis and Chloe. The story opens with a prayer, that the book will bring pleasure and comfort to lovers, and I find that a wonderfully disarming way to begin. The essay draws out the lyrical, musical quality of the prose, and that's why I'm mentioning it to you. It's a reminder that beautiful, melodic writing about love and the countryside is as old as storytelling, and that a book can set out simply to console and delight, without apology. If you ever want a counterweight to the more brooding texts on a syllabus, it might be worth a look.

From the same family of ideas, The Guardian has an essay on the unexpected power of fleeting friendships. It starts from the Russian idea of the poputchik, a stranger met on a journey to whom one confesses everything. There's something rather beautiful about that: the train compartment, the temporary closeness, the freedom of telling a person you'll never see again. The essay moves from Tolstoy's The Kreutzer Sonata, where that very situation sets the story going, towards a reflection on whether we undervalue brief bonds, the ones that don't last but still change us. It's a thoughtful piece about both literature and ordinary life, and the literary side is there throughout, because those travelling confessions are such a good device for a narrator. A stranger on a train is the perfect listener, and the reader gets to eavesdrop.

Literary Hub also has an essay that imagines what William Blake would have made of artificial intelligence. It begins with the word "icon", and how it has travelled from sacred image to the double-clickable thumbnail on a screen. That's a clever way in, and the Blake link ties together painting and poetry, which is just the territory you enjoy. Blake was an engraver and a poet, someone who saw words and images as one act of vision, so he's a natural figure to ask. Whatever one thinks about the subject, the essay is a good reminder that his view of imagination, and of what it means to make something, still seems oddly up to date. It could even work as a starting point for a conversation with older students about how we use images and symbols now.

Last, a little piece of history with a mystery inside it. This week in literary history, Literary Hub remembers the death in the Bastille of the Man in the Iron Mask. He was a prisoner arrested in 1669, during the reign of Louis XIV, and his identity was never revealed. I like this one for the way it shows how a gap in the record becomes the perfect space for fiction. We don't know who he was, and so storytellers have been filling in the blank ever since. For a reader who enjoys learning history through novels, and who lives in France, it's a nice example of a real, unsolved story that kept its hold on the imagination precisely because it can't be answered.

If I were choosing one thread to follow today, it might be Harrison's idea that fiction is about giving people a feeling of something, because it runs quietly through almost everything here, from Longus's lyrical prayer to Mortimer's dying narrator. Whichever you reach for, I hope there's a good page waiting for you with your coffee.

art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the sixteenth of November, and today's art news has a pleasing thread running through it: apocalypses, overlooked women, and a good deal of Belgian shadow.

Let's begin close to home, at the Musée de Grenoble, where there's something this afternoon. At half past two, the Friends of the Museum are holding a session built around Martin Provost's 2023 film about Pierre Bonnard and Marthe. If you like painters' lives rendered as drama, and Marthe being given her due beside him, it could be a lovely way to spend an hour, if you can get away. Yesterday, Sunday, there was also a guided tour of the François Morellet exhibition at the same hour. That has passed, but the title is worth keeping in your pocket: "Sous la géométrie, la facétie", playfulness beneath the geometry. It suggests a man who played with rules, rather than obeying them.

Then, on Wednesday the eighteenth, also at half past two, comes the item I'd mark in your diary. The museum's "Au fil du Texte" series turns to the Apocalypse of Angers, the great medieval tapestry cycle, and to its literary source, the Book of Revelation. It's exactly the kind of talk where a text and its images are read against each other. And the museum's library has put together a selection of books on Anne Truitt, to accompany the exhibition "Libérer la couleur", for anyone who wants to carry on reading beyond the gallery walls. One more local note: l'Essentiel reports on a project near Grenoble called "Onze regards contre le harcèlement de rue", eleven gazes against street harassment, which seems to gather eleven artistic responses. I only have the headline, so I can't say more, but it may be worth a look.

Now, the apocalypse theme has a rather vivid echo in The Guardian this week. The paper reports, in an exclusive, that a sixteenth-century manuscript known as the Book of Miracles may fetch around one million pounds at auction. It holds one hundred and sixty-seven paintings of apocalyptic omens and extreme weather: comets, storms, strange skies. The Guardian's headline calls it the sixteenth-century version of doomscrolling, which is a fine way to put it. Public institutions will have the first chance to bid. Set beside the Angers tapestries, it makes a lovely pairing: two eras, two ways of picturing the end of the world, and perhaps a good prompt for a class on how fear gets turned into images.

A second thread this week is the rescuing of women artists from the margins. The Guardian reports on a new exhibition that puts Mary Cassatt back at the heart of Impressionism. It stresses her friendship with Degas, and her position as a woman and an American outsider in France. In Beaux Arts Magazine, there's a piece on Lucia Moholy, the photographer whose images helped shape how the world saw the Bauhaus, and who also worked on heritage preservation. She is now being put in the spotlight at UNESCO. It's a classic story of a woman whose work was everywhere, while her name was nowhere. And the Bibliothèque nationale de France is presenting sixty years of work by the feminist cartoonist Agnès Rosenstiehl, drawing on a donation of more than seven hundred original drawings. The magazine quotes her line, "Mimi Cracra, c'est moi", which tells you the work is lively and personal, somewhere between drawing, satire and the printed page.

Staying with Beaux Arts Magazine, there's a pleasing Belgian pair. At the Villa Empain in Brussels, an exhibition brings the Symbolist painter Léon Spilliaert back into view. He's best known for his deserted landscapes and tormented self-portraits, and the show apparently looks beyond them. He has a strong, haunting presence, the sort of painter who might sit well beside a gothic narrator. The same magazine also offers a three-minute introduction to Théo Van Rysselberghe, the Belgian neo-impressionist, described as an anarchist, and noted for his international reach. It's a quick, accessible read if he's a name you've half-known.

On painters and their patrons, Hyperallergic has a review of James Cahill's book on David Hockney and his Beverly Hills patron. The relationship between artist and patron is a story in itself, and I'd imagine it makes for good reading. The piece also touches on arts journalism and a Congressional bill, which you can happily skip. Elsewhere, there's an exhibition of recent sculpture by Yoshitomo Nara at Château La Coste, reported by Arts in the City. His figures often have a childlike, melancholy edge, art with a strong emotional voice, if you're ever down that way.

And two last glimpses further afield, both from The Guardian. One is a gallery of five beautiful eco buildings around the world, from a bamboo gym in Bali to an earth house in Wiltshire, including the Children's Village in Tocantins, Brazil: proof that green architecture can be lovely to look at. The other, in pictures, is Powerhouse Parramatta's new exhibition The Mall, which looks at the shopping mall through history and photography, including one hundred new works by Jo Duck and Bahram Mia on western Sydney. It's a long way from Belledonne, but an interesting take on public space.

That's the round-up. I hope the afternoon light is kind, whether you spend it with Bonnard or simply with a good book.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the sixteenth of November, and today's art news begins at the Musée de Grenoble, then drifts through apocalypses, overlooked women and a few haunting painters.

Let me start at home. There are three things at the museum this week, and one has already slipped by. Yesterday afternoon, Sunday, there was a guided tour of the François Morellet exhibition, called "Sous la géométrie, la facétie". That title promises playfulness beneath the geometry, which is a lovely way to describe an artist who builds with lines and rules and still seems to be smiling. The tour has gone, but the exhibition itself is still there, and the title alone makes it a good excuse for a wander.

Today, at half past two, there's a Friends of the Museum session built around Martin Provost's 2023 film "Bonnard, Pierre et Marthe". It's a film about the painter Pierre Bonnard and Marthe, and it suits anyone who enjoys a painter's life rendered as drama rather than as a list of dates. If your afternoon allows it, it's a pleasant way to meet the person behind the colours. If not, it might be worth keeping in mind for the next time Bonnard comes up in conversation, or in the classroom.

The one I'd mark most firmly in your diary is on Wednesday, the eighteenth, again at half past two. It's a talk in the series "Au fil du Texte", on the Apocalypse of Angers. The Apocalypse of Angers is the medieval tapestry cycle, and the talk links it to its literary source, the Book of Revelation. That is exactly the kind of conversation between image and text that you like: a story told in thread, and the written vision that inspired it. For a teacher of literature, there's something appealing about seeing how a text of fire and beasts and trumpets gets translated into something that hangs on a wall, and what is gained and lost on the way.

Staying with the museum, the library there has put together a reading selection on Anne Truitt, to accompany the exhibition "Libérer la couleur". It's a useful thing for anyone who wants to go beyond the walls of the show, to read around the work and let it settle. Truitt is the kind of artist whose work, I suspect, rewards a little reading before or after the visit, and a library list is a gentle way into that.

And one local item from near Grenoble, though I can only give you the headline, from l'Essentiel. It's called "Onze regards contre le harcèlement de rue", eleven gazes against street harassment. It appears to present eleven artistic responses to the subject, but the text I have is only the headline, so I can't tell you where, or in what form. If it catches your eye, it may be worth a look at the local listings.

Now, the apocalypse, which turns out to be having a moment. The Guardian reports on a rare sixteenth-century manuscript called the Book of Miracles, which may fetch around one million pounds at auction. It's a set of one hundred and sixty-seven paintings of apocalyptic omens and extreme weather. Public institutions get the first chance to bid, so there's at least a hope it ends up somewhere people can see it. The headline quotes someone describing it as the sixteenth-century version of doomscrolling, which is rather brilliant, and rather true. Here is a world looking up at strange skies, collecting portents, and finding that it can't look away. Set beside the Angers talk on Wednesday, it makes a neat pairing: one apocalypse stitched in tapestry from a sacred text, another painted, page after page, as a catalogue of dread. For a première class, I can imagine that comparison doing a lot of work, especially when it comes to how people have always tried to make sense of frightening times by turning them into images and stories.

From there, a group of pieces about women who deserve a larger place in the story of their own time.

The Guardian reports on a new exhibition that restores Mary Cassatt to the centre of Impressionism. It stresses her friendship with Degas, and her position as a woman and an American outsider in France. That's a good angle, because it takes a painter often mentioned at the edge of the movement and asks what the movement looks like when she's at its heart. There's a fine account here of an overlooked painter inside a very famous group, and it reminds us how much the standard story of a movement depends on who's doing the telling.

In a similar spirit, Beaux Arts Magazine reports that UNESCO is shining a light on Lucia Moholy. She was a photographer who helped shape the image of the Bauhaus, and she also worked on heritage preservation. So the pictures many of us associate with that famous school owe something to her eye, and yet her name has long stayed in the shadows. It's a good story for anyone interested in the history of modernist design, and in the question of who gets credit for the images that define an era.

And from the same magazine, a lively one: the Bibliothèque nationale de France is presenting sixty years of work by the feminist cartoonist Agnès Rosenstiehl, drawing on a donation of more than seven hundred original drawings. The piece quotes her, "Mimi Cracra, c'est moi!", Mimi Cracra being her best-known character, and it suggests a body of work that is personal, funny and sharp. It sits somewhere between drawing, satire and the printed page, which makes it a nice neighbour to literature. If you're ever looking for a way to bring humour and a feminist voice into a lesson about narrators, a cartoonist who says that her character is herself is a rather good place to begin.

Now to the painters with a strong, haunting presence. In Brussels, at the Villa Empain, an exhibition is bringing the Symbolist painter Léon Spilliaert back into view. Beaux Arts Magazine says it goes beyond the deserted landscapes and tormented self-portraits for which he's known. Those two phrases alone, deserted landscapes and tormented self-portraits, tell you a good deal about the mood. The setting is a sumptuous villa, and the contrast between that grandeur and the loneliness of the paintings sounds striking. He seems to be an artist for anyone who loves atmosphere, the kind of painter whose work feels like a narrator speaking quietly in an empty room.

The same magazine offers a short introduction to another Belgian, Théo Van Rysselberghe, in a three-minute read. He was a neo-impressionist painter, described as an anarchist, with an international reach. If the name is not one you know well, this is a quick and accessible way to meet him, and the combination of anarchist and neo-impressionist, of political conviction and carefully placed dabs of colour, is an intriguing one.

Turning to Hyperallergic, there's a review of James Cahill's book about David Hockney and his Beverly Hills patron. That relationship between painter and patron is a fascinating one, a mixture of friendship, money and the pull of a place, and it fits well with your interest in the stories behind pictures. The same piece also touches on arts journalism and a Congressional bill, which I'll leave aside, but the Hockney portion is the part worth your time.

And in the south of France, Arts in the City notes an exhibition of recent sculpture by Yoshitomo Nara at Château La Coste. Nara's work often has a childlike and melancholy edge, and it carries a strong emotional voice. I don't have more detail than that, but if you like art that speaks in a very particular tone, tender and a little sad, it may be one to keep an eye on for a trip.

Two last items, both a little further from home, and both about space and how we live in it.

The Guardian has a piece on five beautiful eco buildings around the world, under the quote "it's an architect's dream". They range from a bamboo gym in Bali to an earth house in Wiltshire, and include the Children's Village in Tocantins, Brazil. The point is that green architecture can be beautiful as well as responsible. It's more about design and climate than about art history, but there's something pleasing about buildings made of bamboo and earth, materials that feel almost like sentences in a very old language.

And finally, again from The Guardian, a photo gallery from Powerhouse Parramatta in Sydney. Their new exhibition, The Mall, looks at the shopping mall through history and photography. It includes one hundred new works by Jo Duck and Bahram Mia on western Sydney. It's a long way from the Grésivaudan, but the idea is an interesting one: that a place we pass through without thinking, a mall, can be looked at as a kind of public square, with its own stories and its own characters.

So, if I had to pick a thread for the week, it would be the Apocalypse of Angers on Wednesday, with the Book of Miracles in your head as a companion. And if the afternoon is kind, a little Bonnard today.

Enjoy the quieter hours of the Monday, Yamuna, and may the only apocalypse you meet be a tapestry one.

around.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter stretch for village fairs, but the calendar around Grenoble is filling up nicely with theatre, music and exhibitions as we head towards December.

Let me start close to home, with two things that have just finished. Yesterday afternoon, in your own village, the Salle Pelloux-Prayer in Les Adrets hosted a screening for the Mois du Doc, a documentary called Tero Loko, cultiver l'accueil, from five to half past seven. The listing says little about the film itself, but it is nice to know that documentary evenings are happening on your doorstep. Also yesterday, the second contemporary art fair at the Maison des Arts in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin came to a close. If you missed it, there is a second chance to see art there. Le Grésivaudan announces an exhibition by the intercommunal artothèque, the art lending library, in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin. The listing gives no dates, so do check before you go. It could be a pleasant way to look at the paintings and prints that local people borrow and hang in their homes.

Staying with exhibitions, there is a free display in Grenoble about the military high-mountain group, the Groupe militaire de haute montagne. It runs until the thirty-first of December, so there is plenty of time. The description is short, but it sounds like a small piece of mountain history, which feels very much of this region. Also in Grenoble, the website jds.fr reports that an immersive light-and-sound show built around water is coming to a museum in the city. No dates are given in the teaser, so it is one to watch for.

The MC2 in Grenoble is where most of the activity is, so let me take you through it in order. On Thursday the nineteenth and Friday the twentieth of November, there is L'Ange du foyer, a theatre piece by Emma Dante, a director whose work is often built around strong ensemble characters. The listing gives no more detail than that. On the Thursday, the nineteenth, there is also Último helecho, a music show by Nina Laisné, François Chaignud and Nadia Larcher. The listing is brief, but the pairing of voice and performance suggests something worth seeing, and it makes for a rich evening if you wanted to combine the two nights.

A week later, on Thursday the twenty-sixth of November, the jazz musician Anne Paceo brings her Atlantis to the MC2. It is a good option for an evening of contemporary jazz close to home.

Into December now. On the third, the MC2 hosts an open studio session of RODA with Aina Alegre. Details are sparse, but a studio showing is a nice chance to see work before it is fully finished. Then comes the one I suspect may interest you most. From the ninth to the eleventh of December, the MC2 stages Article 353 du code pénal, by Tanguy Viel and Emmanuel Noblet. It is a literary text brought to the stage, which could suit a reader who loves fiction in performance. On the tenth, the second of three Le monde en musiques encounter sessions also takes place at the MC2. The description is brief, but it is another musical event within easy reach of Grenoble.

Slightly further along the valley, in Meylan, the Hexagone Scène nationale presents Point de bascule by Le Gravillon on Wednesday the sixteenth of December at eight in the evening. It runs for one hour forty, and follows a researcher who cycles and an offer from Air France to offset his carbon emissions. There is one further date, though the listing doesn't say when.

Closer to everyday life, Ici-Grenoble.org invites readers to the launch evening of Gragenda 2027 in Grenoble, with a magic show, a concert and workshops. There is no date in the text, so look at the listing first. And in Pontcharra, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that the town will celebrate its sporting champions and its volunteers on the eighteenth of November, this Wednesday. The text is short, but it is a warm piece of local community life, just down the valley from you.

Finally, for a breath of air, Le Dauphiné Libéré says the Club Alpin Français suggests the lac du Pontet, at Le Gua, as a lovely walk. The text is brief, but it sounds like a simple outing that could suit a weekend stroll before winter properly arrives.

That's your lot for today, Yamuna, so I hope something in there tempts you out of the house this week.

Now, something for the coming days, closer to the community side of life. On Wednesday the eighteenth of November, the town of Pontcharra will hold a celebration for its sporting champions and its volunteers. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports it, though briefly. Moving into Grenoble itself, there are a few things that are not tied to a single evening and which you can fit around your teaching timetable. The first is a free display on the Groupe militaire de haute montagne, the army's high-mountain unit, which runs in Grenoble until the thirty-first of December. It is listed by Isère Attractivité, and the extract gives little detail beyond that. But since it's free and open until the end of the year, it's an easy one to slot in on a free afternoon. The second is something I'm rather curious about. The website jds.fr reports that an immersive light-and-sound show built around water is coming to a Grenoble museum, under the title Lumières au musée. The teaser gives no dates, so I can't say when. But the idea of a museum being transformed by light and sound around the theme of water is an appealing one, and it's worth keeping an eye out for the dates.

And while we're on Grenoble, Ici-Grenoble.org carries an invitation to the launch evening of the Gragenda 2027. The evening promises a magic show, a concert and workshops. No date is given in the text, so please check the listing before you go. It sounds like a lively, slightly playful evening, and a good way to begin planning the year's outings.

Now to the largest cluster of events, the MC2 in Grenoble, which has a rich run of performances over the next month. I'll take them in the order they fall.

The first is this Thursday, the nineteenth of November, and it's a double. On the Thursday and Friday, the nineteenth and twentieth, the MC2 presents L'Ange du foyer, a theatre piece by Emma Dante. The listing gives no further detail, but Dante is a director whose work is often built around strong ensemble characters, which I think would suit your taste for stories driven by people rather than plot machinery. On the same Thursday evening, the nineteenth, the MC2 also presents Último helecho, a music show by Nina Laisné, François Chaignaud and Nadia Larcher. The listing is brief, but the pairing of voice and performance suggests something worth seeing. So if you wanted to choose between the two on Thursday, it would be between a theatre piece and a music show, and I'm afraid the listing doesn't say more than that to help you decide.

The week after, on Thursday the twenty-sixth of November, the MC2 hosts the jazz drummer and composer Anne Paceo, performing Atlantis. The listing describes it as a concert of contemporary jazz. It's a good option for an evening of music close to home, and the date is a Thursday, which may suit a working week better than a weekend.

Into December, on the third, there is an open studio session at the MC2 for RODA, with Aina Alegre. An open studio is a chance to see work in progress rather than a finished show, and since I know you enjoy dance and music documentaries, there might be something for you in watching a creative process at close quarters. The extract gives few details, so it would be wise to check what the session involves.

Then comes the literary item I think you'll like most. From the ninth to the eleventh of December, the MC2 stages Article 353 du code pénal, a theatre adaptation of Tanguy Viel's work, directed and performed by Emmanuel Noblet. Viel's text is a literary one brought to the stage, so this is fiction in performance, which could make it a nice companion for a reader who enjoys strong narrators. If you teach or recommend French novels to your students, it might even be a talking point for a lesson. The run is three evenings, so there's some room to choose.

On the tenth of December, the middle of that run, the MC2 also holds the second of three encounter sessions called Le monde en musiques, the world in music. The description is brief, so I can't tell you what the session contains, but the title, and the fact that it's the second in a series of three, suggest a thread you could follow if the first caught your interest.

One more venue, slightly outside the city. On Wednesday the sixteenth of December at eight in the evening, the Hexagone, the Scène nationale in Meylan, presents Point de bascule by the company Le Gravillon. It runs for an hour and forty minutes. The piece follows a researcher who is also a cyclist, and who is offered, by Air France, a way to offset his carbon dioxide emissions. The listing mentions one further date, though doesn't say when, so it's worth checking if the sixteenth doesn't suit. It sounds like a story with a very particular central character, and a quietly comic dilemma at its heart.

So, in order, to gather the dates: the eighteenth in Pontcharra, the nineteenth and twentieth for Emma Dante, the nineteenth for Último helecho, the twenty-sixth for Anne Paceo, the third of December for RODA, the ninth to the eleventh for Article 353, the tenth for the music encounter, and the sixteenth in Meylan. A good many of these come with very short descriptions, so before you buy a ticket, a quick look at the venue's own page will tell you more than I can.

That's the picture for the week, Yamuna, and I hope something in it tempts you out of the house, perhaps with a scarf and a flask for that lake walk.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter day for the BFI corner, but there's a cluster of Hamlet coverage, a Blake essay with a timely angle, and a few Atwood and Orwell threads worth knowing about.

Let me start with Hamlet, since that's where most of the news is. A production called Hamlet Hail to the Thief is at the Barbican, and it has been reviewed by two outlets in the last couple of days. Theatre and Tonic has a review of the Barbican staging. Liam O'Dell, in his own review, calls it a dark and noisy spectacle in which Shakespeare's Hamlet collides with the music of Radiohead. The London Evening Standard has also run a feature on how Shakespeare and Radiohead came together to make the piece. I only have the outline of each, not the full text, so I can't tell you how the adaptation handles the verse or the soliloquies. But as a pair, the reviews give you a ready-made way into a question your première pupils might enjoy. What happens to a play when its language is partly replaced, or surrounded, by contemporary music? Hamlet is on the 2027 session list, so it's a good moment to have a modern, loud, risky staging to set beside the text. You could put a review extract on the board and ask whether "noisy" is a fair word for a play that is already full of noise, from the ghost on the battlements to the madness of Ophelia.

Staying with Shakespeare for a moment, TAPinto announces that Shakespeare & Company is presenting its thirty-eighth Fall Festival of Shakespeare, from the nineteenth to the twenty-second of November. The notice doesn't say where, so it's mainly a sign of how alive the tradition is, rather than something you could attend. Still, thirty-eight years of a festival is a nice fact to offer a class.

Now to Blake. Literary Hub has an essay titled "What Would William Blake Have Thought of AI?" All I have is the headline, so I can't say what it argues. But Songs of Innocence and of Experience is on the 2027 programme, and the question is a rich one. Blake wrote about mills, machines and the "mind-forged manacles" of his age, and he distrusted systems that flatten the imagination. Even without the essay, you could use the title as a discussion prompt with seconde or première: which of the Songs would feel most at home in a conversation about artificial intelligence, and why? It might be worth a quick read yourself to see whether it's classroom material.

On to Orwell and Atwood, who link nicely to the oral themes list. The BBC has a piece on how Kent may have inspired Orwell's Animal Farm. Again, I only have the headline. Animal Farm isn't itself on your list, but Orwell is there through 1984, and a piece about how a real landscape can feed a fable is a good thing to have in your pocket when pupils ask where a writer gets an idea. It's also the sort of story you like, where a novel is tied to a real place and to history.

Atwood is in the news twice. CBC reports that Margaret Atwood is joining other bird lovers to oppose a proposed six-hundred-foot tower on Pelee Island. I have only the headline, so no more detail than that, but it's a pleasing reminder of the author behind The Handmaid's Tale as a public voice for the natural world, which is a thread you can pull in her fiction too. Separately, Broadcast Dialogue reports that The Testaments, the sequel to The Handmaid's Tale, was one of the leading winners at the twenty twenty-six DGC Awards, alongside Small Achievable Goals. That's a Canadian awards report, and I only have the headline, but it confirms that Atwood's world continues to be adapted and noticed. If you teach The Handmaid's Tale for the oral, it's a small piece of context on its afterlife.

Related to that, The Conversation has a piece looking at six post-apocalyptic novels and how differently they imagine the collapse of the world. The text doesn't give the titles, so I can't say whether any are on your list. But the oral themes include The Road and Parable of the Sower, and the question the article poses, that collapse can look very different from one writer to the next, is exactly the comparison an oral candidate might be asked to make. It could be worth reading to see which novels it picks, and whether it offers a useful contrast with McCarthy's bleakness or Butler's more constructive imagination.

A few items sit at the edge of the syllabus but might interest you as a reader. Book Riot has a list of the best fiction of the century so far. I only have the title, so I can't judge the selection, but lists like this are handy for spotting recent novels to recommend to keen pupils. Dawn has a short piece of fiction called "The Past Is Picture-Perfect", apparently about memory and how the past is remembered. Its quality is unknown, but the title alone, with its play on photographs and the past, would make a lovely creative-writing prompt. And The Sunday Guardian asks when the new Pride and Prejudice adaptation, with Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden, will arrive online. There's no release date in the text, so it's really a streaming notice, though Austen's Emma is on your oral list, and pupils may well be watching.

Finally, two warm local-theatre stories, neither connected to the BFI but both pleasant. In Newry, an actor is backing the name of Sean Hollywood for a new theatre, as reported by Newry.ie. And in the Berkshires, iBerkshires reports on the Berkies, which honour regional theatre talent. It's good news from a long way off, about people who make theatre in their own communities.

That's the round-up, Yamuna, and I hope the day treats you as kindly as a good soliloquy treats its audience.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter couple of days for official BFI news, with no new texts or reforms to report, but there's a good cluster of Hamlet material, a few useful hooks for the oral themes, and some theatre stories to round things off.

Let me begin with the biggest thread, which is Hamlet on stage. Hamlet is on the 2027 session programme, and three pieces this weekend are about the same production, or at least what looks like the same one. It's called Hamlet Hail to the Thief, and it sets Shakespeare's play alongside the music of Radiohead. Theatre and Tonic has reviewed it at the Barbican, and a second review, by Liam O'Dell, calls it a dark and noisy spectacle in which Radiohead and Shakespeare collide. The London Evening Standard has a feature on how Shakespeare and Radiohead came together to create the work, and it's the Standard's headline that calls it a theatrical masterpiece. I'd stay a little careful there, since that's the paper's framing, and I've only had the headline and short descriptions to go on rather than the full text of each piece.

Still, even from those descriptions, there's something worth taking into the classroom. The idea of a Hamlet driven by contemporary music is a lovely way into the question of adaptation: what does a modern audience hear in the play that a Jacobean one might not? A dark and noisy staging suggests a production that leans into the play's unrest, its sense of a court where something is rotten, and that gives you a nice point of comparison with the text itself. You might ask students to look at a soliloquy on the page, then think about what sound, silence or volume would do to it. Is "To be or not to be" better in a hush or against a wall of noise? You don't need to have seen the production to set that question, and the reviews could serve as short readings for older students who like to see how critics describe staging choices. For première, it might also be a gentle introduction to reading a theatre review as a genre in itself, with its own vocabulary of spectacle, tone and interpretation.

Staying with Shakespeare, TAPinto reports that Shakespeare & Company is presenting its thirty-eighth Fall Festival of Shakespeare from the nineteenth to the twenty-second of November. The text I have doesn't say where it takes place, so I can't tell you whether it's anywhere you could get to, and it's mainly an event notice. But it's a small reminder that Shakespeare festivals have long lives of their own, and thirty-eight years is a nice figure to drop into a conversation about why these plays keep being staged.

Now to the other set texts, and a pair of pieces that connect the programme to the wider world. The first is from Literary Hub, an essay with the title "What Would William Blake Have Thought of AI?" Songs of Innocence and of Experience is on the 2027 programme, and I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what the essay argues. But the question itself is a good one for a class. Blake was writing about industry, about the mind and its constraints, about what it means to make things and to see clearly, and he wrote of "mind-forged manacles" in "London". Students will find it natural to bring their own views about technology into a conversation about a poet who was suspicious of systems that shrink the imagination. It might work well as a short debate task: take a poem from Experience, such as "London" or "The Tyger", and ask what Blake might say to a machine that writes. Whether or not the essay turns out to be as useful as the headline promises, the premise gives you a bridge between a poet from the late seventeen hundreds and the world your students actually live in.

The second piece is from the BBC, on how Kent may have inspired Orwell's Animal Farm. Again, I only have the headline, so I can't say what places or details the article points to. Animal Farm isn't on the programme, but Orwell's 1984 is among the oral themes, and a piece that roots a famous fable in a real landscape is the kind of thing you tend to enjoy: fiction that grows out of a place and a moment in history. If the article is good, it might be a nice short reading to set beside 1984, as a way of asking how much of Orwell's imagined world comes from somewhere he actually stood.

Margaret Atwood is in the news too, though not for a book. CBC reports that she is joining other bird lovers to fight a proposed six-hundred-foot tower on Pelee Island. The Handmaid's Tale is one of the oral themes works, so it's a nice human note about its author, who is evidently as committed to the natural world in real life as her fiction often is to the consequences of human choices. I only have the headline, so the details are thin, but it might be a pleasant thing to mention to a class when you introduce her. Related to that, Broadcast Dialogue reports that The Testaments, the sequel to The Handmaid's Tale, was one of the leading winners at the twenty twenty-six DGC Awards, alongside Small Achievable Goals. Again, that's from a headline alone, so I can't tell you which categories or what the awards recognised. But it's a useful reminder that Gilead keeps finding new audiences, which may help if you have students who know the story from the screen before they open the book.

Then there are a few pieces for the oral themes list and for general reading. The Conversation has an article looking at six post-apocalyptic novels and how differently each imagines the collapse of the world. The text I have doesn't name the books, so I can't confirm whether any are on the programme. But two of your oral themes works, The Road and Parable of the Sower, sit squarely in that territory, and the framing of the piece, that these novels imagine collapse very differently, is a good prompt for comparison. Cormac McCarthy's bleak, stripped-back world and Octavia Butler's more social, community-building vision are about as different as two imagined endings can be, and students often respond to being asked which feels more plausible, and which more hopeful. You could use the article as a starting point and let students see whether the writer's ideas match their own reading.

Book Riot has a list of the best fiction books of the century so far. I only have the title, so I can't judge the selection, but lists like this can be handy when you're looking for recent novels to recommend to a keen reader in première, or to add to your own pile. And Dawn has published a short piece of fiction called "The Past Is Picture-Perfect", apparently about memory and how we remember the past. That is all I know, and its quality is unknown, but the title alone chimes with a lot of what you teach: unreliable memory is a theme in Atonement and The Go-Between, both on the oral themes list, and a short story about a too-perfect past could prompt a good discussion about nostalgia and narration. If it turns out to be good, it may be worth reading as a class.

On the adaptation front, The Sunday Guardian asks when a new Pride and Prejudice adaptation starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden will reach streaming. There's no release date in the text, so it's really a streaming notice. Pride and Prejudice isn't on the programme, though Emma is among the oral themes, and any new Austen adaptation is a fair excuse to talk with students about how screen versions choose what to keep and what to cut. It may be one to watch for when the date is announced.

Finally, two warm theatre stories from further afield, neither with a direct link to the BFI, but pleasant to end on. In Northern Ireland, Newry.ie reports that a Newry actor is backing the use of Sean Hollywood's name for a new theatre in the town. The text is brief, but it's a lovely little story about a community deciding to honour one of its own by naming a stage after him. And in the Berkshires, iBerkshires.com reports on the Berkies, which honour regional theatre talent. It's a cheerful reminder that a great deal of theatre happens far from the big London stages, in local halls, by people who simply love it.

That's the round-up for today. A good week, perhaps, to let Hamlet and Blake do the heavy lifting in class, with Atwood and the post-apocalyptic novels waiting in the wings. Have a lovely day, and I hope the Belledonne air is as crisp as the autumn deserves.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the sixteenth of November, and here is a gentle round-up of France over the last two days, with a fair bit for a teacher and a few things for a reader.

Let me start close to home. Franceinfo reports that Michel Destot, the Socialist mayor of Grenoble from nineteen ninety-five to twenty fourteen, and for a time MP for the Isère's third constituency, died on the fourteenth of November, aged eighty. He was a familiar name in the city for nearly two decades, so you may well hear it spoken about this week.

Now to schools, which dominate the news. The Guardian reports that France has entered its eighth week of student protests over school buildings, teacher shortages and related demands. Some teachers are losing patience, with the paper quoting the feeling that it is time to get back to class. Pupils facing exams have, in some cases, missed up to a hundred and fifty hours of lessons. Franceinfo adds that a prefecture order published on Sunday bans gatherings and marches within a hundred metres of several lycées and universities in Paris and its surrounding region, with the authorities citing the risk of damage and fires. La Mire's daily television zapping touches on the same world. The edition for Saturday the fourteenth looks at headteachers across France, including a mortar attack in Lyon and a school set on fire, along with the debate about teachers' complicity and the student blockades. Sunday's edition, by contrast, turns to the large Acte Five protests, and includes the rather lovely detail of an orchestra playing within a demonstration in Lyon. It ends on a light feature about Iceland, where knitting is a men's affair, which is a pleasant way to close.

If you want a change of perspective on school life, franceinfo has a piece asking whether Estonia's teaching conditions could be a model for France. It looks at professional autonomy for teachers, what the French call pedagogical freedom, and at pay that is partly linked to merit. It is written for a French audience, but it may be interesting to set beside your own experience of different systems.

On the weather, there has been heavy rain and flooding in the Hérault. Franceinfo says hundreds of motorists were trapped around Montpellier on the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth of November, and about a hundred were brought to safety. One seventy-three-year-old driver who had been reported missing was found safe and well, which is the good news in an otherwise soggy story.

Turning to books and culture, there are three pieces you might enjoy. First, a review on franceinfo of "Jupiter", a geopolitical thriller by Alexandre Smia. It imagines France, the European Union's only nuclear power, weighing whether to use its arsenal in the conflict between Ukraine and Russia. The reviewer calls it breathtaking. The premise is weighty, but it is a thriller, and you like those. Second, the critic Christelle Bakima-Poundza has written a hybrid essay called "Aya, pour l'exemple", on Aya Nakamura and the cultures that paved her way in France. She presents it as a portrait of a France with unlimited dreams, and it sounds like writing that sets culture in its wider social picture. Third, a more sobering watch: "Inside Gaza", by the director Hélène Lam Trong, follows the daily work of AFP reporters in Gaza. It has won the Doc Edge prize in New Zealand, and the Grand prix at a French festival of reportage and social documentary. It is serious, of course, but sounds like a considered piece of documentary-making.

There is also an exhibition story with a literary flavour. Louis Vuitton is presenting "La Valise", a book and exhibition by the photographer and director Bruno Aveillan. It is built around one Alzer suitcase that he used over thirteen years of travel. It is brand-backed, certainly, but the idea of a single object tracing a long journey is a nice one, and it does read a little like a story told through things.

And now a few lighter touches. Organisers of the Salon international de l'agriculture have chosen Seraffine, a red-dusted Auvergne cow, as the face of the twenty twenty-seven edition. Franceinfo quotes a description of her as having "une jolie robe rouge poudrée", a pretty powdery red coat. She is a happy return for cattle, since in twenty twenty-five no animals were shown because of the nodular dermatosis health crisis. Also on franceinfo, a warm behind-the-scenes look at a French company's training course for Pères Noël. They learn how to answer children's questions and how to properly inhabit the role, and one trainee says they are there to spread the magic of the festive season, which is very important. It is a small seasonal craft, nicely observed.

The Local France has a reader poll that has named a favourite French cheese. The text I have doesn't say which one won, so you will have to open the full article to find out, which is a small suspense in itself. The Local also offers its French expression of the day, "se gourer". It is an informal verb meaning to get something wrong or be mistaken. It is handy in everyday conversation, and might make a neat example for a class on register, set against something more formal like "se tromper".

That is the round-up for today, and I hope your Monday is calm, dry, and entirely free of anyone having to say "je me suis gouré".

Good morning, Yamuna. This is a good news briefing with a pleasing number of stories about people being quietly brave, kind or stubbornly creative, and several of them might be of particular interest to a teacher of literature.

Let me begin with the past, since a few of this morning's stories are about people who were overlooked and then, eventually, seen.

The Good News Network tells the story of Ada Le Poidevin, a shopkeeper on Guernsey during the Second World War. Her diaries, written in those years, reveal that she hid three British soldiers who had been left behind after a raid, keeping them out of the hands of the Nazis. What makes the story so striking is the timing. Her bravery only came to light forty years after her death, through her own words, written at the time. It reads like the opening of a novel: an ordinary woman behind a shop counter, an occupied island, and a secret kept in plain sight. It is also a lovely example of what you often say about fiction, that history lands harder when it comes through one person's voice rather than a list of dates. A diary is a narrator, after all, and this one has been waiting decades for readers. It might make a fine companion text for a class studying first-person accounts of war, or simply a story to tell on a quiet Monday.

Two other stories this morning are about women restored to their rightful place in the history of art. The Guardian reports on a new exhibition that puts Mary Cassatt back at the heart of Impressionism. The show emphasises her friendship with Degas, and it looks at her position as both a woman and an American outsider working in France. She has too often been treated as a footnote to a famous movement, and the Guardian describes the exhibition as a fine account of an overlooked painter. For someone who enjoys the conversation between paintings and written works, it is an invitation to think about how an outsider's eye can see a familiar world differently, which is, of course, what many of the best narrators do.

Then there is Lucia Moholy, who is the subject of attention at UNESCO, according to Beaux Arts Magazine. She was a photographer, and she helped shape the image we have of the Bauhaus, the way the school and its buildings and objects look to us today. She also worked on the preservation of heritage. The magazine calls her a little-known pioneer, and the recognition at UNESCO feels like a correction long overdue. If you enjoy those stories where a figure stands just outside the frame of a famous movement and turns out to have helped draw the frame itself, this is one of them. There are clear links here to the history of modernist design, which could be a lovely thread to follow if you ever want to bring images and texts of the period together.

On the literary front, NPR reports that M. John Harrison has become the first science fiction author to win the Booker Prize. It is a milestone for a genre that has so often been kept at the margins of literary prizes, and NPR suggests it is also a good way into his work. Whatever one thinks of such divisions between genres, there is something cheering about a barrier coming down. If any of your pupils have ever been told that the books they love are not proper literature, this might be a useful piece of news to carry into the classroom.

And, for a lighter note in the cultural corner, Upworthy tells the story of how Blur, in nineteen ninety-seven, recorded a two-minute song as a prank on their record label. The joke did not go as planned, because the song became one of the defining anthems of the decade. It is a small, affectionate anecdote about how the things we do not take seriously sometimes turn out to be the things people remember. Your older pupils may well know the tune even if they were born long after it came out.

Let me turn now to stories of people looking after one another, which this morning are many.

Upworthy has the story of Brian Schwartz, who lost his job and, rather than simply waiting for the next thing, began mowing lawns for free. That small act of generosity has grown into a nationwide network of around two thousand one hundred volunteers, all connecting neighbours with practical help. There is something very concrete about it. Nobody is being asked to change the world, only to cut a neighbour's grass, and yet two thousand people have joined in. It is a good reminder that kindness often begins as a response to one's own difficulty, and spreads because it is so easy to join.

Also from Upworthy, there is a story I found quite moving. Brooklyn Dotson received a liver transplant as a baby, and the donor was a ten-year-old boy. Years later, in September, she married his younger brother, Noah Waters. A gift given in the hardest of circumstances has become, in time, a bond between two families, and now a marriage. I will not try to say more than the facts allow, but it is the sort of true story that novelists would hesitate to invent, in case readers found it too neat.

And then there is a love story of a more leisurely kind. The Good News Network tells of David, an English teenager who, in nineteen ninety-four, was on holiday on the Greek island of Kos. There, a group of children formed a close circle, and among them was a girl called Jodie. The piece follows how, thirty-two years later, Jodie became his wife. The story begins with pen pals and a summer friendship, and it unfolds across three decades. It is warm, character-led, and has the shape of a slow-burning novel, with the long gap in the middle doing so much of the work.

One more from the Good News Network, and it is a gentle one. Paul and Ruth Richmond-Watson are a married couple who are both autistic and have ADHD. Since September they have taken up cleaning grimy street signs, and they hope to travel the country until every sign is spotless. The text I have is cut short, so I cannot tell you much more, but the heart of it is clear: a shared hobby that suits them both, and that quietly improves everyone else's walk down the road. I rather like the idea of a quest so modest and so complete. Next time you pass a street sign in the valley, you may look at it with fresh eyes.

Now to health, where there are three stories this morning, each practical and each with real human stakes.

The first is a medical first. The Good News Network reports that doctors at Franciscan Health, a Catholic health system in the American Midwest, say they have carried out the first bone marrow transplant to treat a non-malignant disease. The donor marrow came from a deceased organ donor, and the patient was a forty-year-old woman with aplastic anaemia. That is a condition in which the bone marrow stops producing enough blood cells. The description of it as a first comes from the doctors themselves, so it is worth holding it with that in mind, but the outcome is reported as a success, and it opens a possible new route for patients who might otherwise have had few options.

The second is a smaller, quieter gain. The Optimist Daily writes about Neupulse, a prototype wrist device for people with Tourette's. In a trial run by the University of Nottingham in twenty twenty-three, with one hundred and twenty-one people in the United Kingdom, the device reduced the frequency of tics by an average of twenty-five percent. A quarter may not sound dramatic, but for someone living with frequent tics, it can mean a great deal in daily life. The Optimist Daily now returns to the subject three years on, and reports how users describe it. It is a good example of a practical advance that does not need to be a miracle to matter.

The third is about place rather than technology. Reasons to be Cheerful has a feature on Against Da Grain, a barbershop on the North Shore of Staten Island, and on how the trust built between barbers and their customers might help improve the health of Black men. The idea is simple and rather lovely: people already talk openly in a barber's chair, and that trust can be put to good use. Now, to nature, which this morning offers two hopeful stories.

If you like a tale with an unlikely hero, a beaver in the desert is hard to beat.

To close, one story about public space, closer to the sort of thing we might enjoy in our own valley. The Good News Network reports that Brian Chesky, the chief executive of Airbnb, has given one hundred million dollars to San Francisco's parks. That is the news for this morning, and I hope it keeps you company on the way down to the valley and perhaps to a good cup of tea afterwards.

To finish on a lighter note, the organisers of the twenty twenty-seven Salon international de l'agriculture have chosen their star: Seraffine, a cow from the Auvergne in what franceinfo calls a pretty powdered red dress. The choice comes after twenty twenty-five, when no cattle were shown because of the nodular dermatosis health crisis, so she is a cheerful sign of country life carrying on.

That's all for today, Yamuna. I hope your Monday is full of good sentences and unexpected stories.
